items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the public health law and the general business law, in relation to the warranting of certain medical devices
items.lawCode: Amd §2803, Pub Health L; add Art 30-B §§645 - 648, Gen Bus L
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S5566

TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public health law and the general business law, in
relation to the warranting of certain medical devices

PURPOSE:

To require sellers of certain medical devices to provide an express
warranty that their product is fit for the ordinary purpose for which
such device is used

SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section one adds a new Public Health Law § 2803(8-b) to require the
Commissioner of Health to establish procedures for hospitals to notify
patients receiving electronic medical devices or implantable hip or knee
medical devices, that such devices are warranted for a period of at
least five years.

Section two adds a new Article 30-B to the General Business Law estab-
lishing the medical device warranty. This section requires the initial
seller of an electronic medical device, defined as an implantable
medical device that requires a battery or similar power source to func-
tion, or an implantable hip or knee medical device, to provide each
consumer of such device with a warranty that the device is fit for its
ordinary purpose and free from defect for a period of at least five
years after it is first used, attached or applied to the consumer. The
seller shall be liable for all costs incurred by the consumer or his or
her insurer to make repairs and replacements for any device that fails
to conform with these provisions upon the report of such nonconformity
or defect. This section also clarifies that nothing in this Article
shall in any way limit the rights, remedies or privileges otherwise
available in law or equity and prohibits the waiver of this warranty.

Section three provides that the act shall take effect on the first of
January next succeeding the date on which it becomes law and applies to
all devices used, attached or applied on or after such date.

JUSTIFICATION:

Manufacturers and sellers of medical devices have an obligation to
ensure their products are safe for use by consumers, especially when
those devices are being implanted. Likewise, consumers should have
confidence in the devices their surgeon is implanting. This legislation
will hold manufacturers accountable by requiring certain medical devices
be expressly warranted as fit for the purpose they are intended. Under
this legislation, an electronic medical device that relies on a battery
to function and implantable hip or knee devices are expressly warranted
for a period of at least five years.  These types of devices are
reported to have the highest rates of failure, defect or recall. Holding

manufacturers accountable will enhance the safety of products and ulti-
mately lead to a decrease in product recalls. This warranty will also
provide consumers with an additional remedy to ensure they are not
financially responsible for any consequences resulting from a defective
medical device.

Recent product recalls, and controversial lawsuits that followed, have
highlighted the need for this legislation. In August 2010, DePuy Ortho-
paedics issued a recall of its ASRTM XL Acetabular Hip System and DePuy
ASRTM Hip Resurfacing System. The New York Times reported that about
93,000 patients, about one-third of them in the United States, received
an ASR. The ASR hip device utilized a metal ball and cup, which report-
edly sheds metallic debris as it wears, this can result in tissue damage
and even crippling injuries. The average artificial hip should last
about 15 years or more before needing to be replaced, where as DePuy
projections estimated that the ASR hip would fail in 40% of patients
within five years. DePuy reportedly began phasing out the ASR when the
FDA asked for more safety information about the implant in 2009, but
continued to sell existing inventories. While DePuy claims they recalled
the ASR after "receiving new, then-unpublished data from a joint
replacement registry in the UK," documents disclosed at trial allegedly
showed that officials were long aware that the flawed design resulted in
premature failure at a high rate.

DePuy Orthopaedics is not alone. With regard to metal-on-metal hip
implants alone, the FDA has recalled two other products, the Smith &
Nephew R3 Metal Liners of the R3 Acetabular System and the Zimmer Duromù
Acetabular Component. This legislation will help to ensure medical
device manufacturers are diligent in guaranteeing the safety of their
products and help to decrease recalls, meanwhile protecting the consumer
when product defects do occur.

LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None.

EFFECTIVE DATE:

Takes effect on the first of January next succeeding the date on which
it becomes law and applies to all devices used, attached or applied on
or after such date.
